opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it's harder than people assume, and it's not mainly about money. Many organizations have the compute. What's rare is the willingness to commit to world-model pre-training as a first-class research problem rather than a side project attached to a language model.

Right now the gravity in the industry pulls almost everything toward LLMs. The scaling recipe for language is known, the products are clear, and the revenue story is easy to tell. So in most big labs, vision or world modeling ends up serving the language model. It becomes a multimodal add-on, an encoder you plug in, or a video generator built for a product demo. That's different from saying: we believe the foundation of intelligence is learning how the physical world works, and we'll build the pre-training stack around that.

To do it properly, an organization needs a few things at once. First, real conviction from leadership, because the payoff is long-term and the path isn't as legible as next-token prediction. Second, people who understand both representation learning and large-scale systems. Those are still somewhat separate communities, and you need them in the same room. Third, freedom to explore objectives that aren't just pixel reconstruction or generation. Rendering beautiful video is not the same as having a model that understands dynamics, causality, and what happens when you act. And fourth, data strategy. The world gives you huge amounts of video and sensory data, but it's messy, and figuring out what to learn from it is a research question in itself.

So the prospects? I'm cautiously optimistic. Over the past year or two, more people have come to agree that language alone won't get us there, and that's a real shift. But I don't think the answer will come from simply adding a world-model team inside an LLM company. It probably requires a place built from day one around this belief, one that's patient, open about its research, and willing to be wrong for a while. That's partly why I've thought so much about where to spend my own time. If you really believe in this direction, at some point you have to create the environment where it can actually be done, not just wait for one to appear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute availability and the industry’s focus on LLMs, but does not attribute robotics startups’ lack of capacity to resources being consumed by scaling robot hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a genuinely open question, and I'd resist the idea that it has to be one kind of organization.

If you look at what world-model pre-training actually requires, it's a different profile from language model pre-training. Language had this gift: the internet already contained trillions of tokens of human-curated, compressed knowledge. Video and embodied data are abundant, but they're low-density. Most frames are redundant, and the signal you care about, the physics, the causality, the long-horizon structure, is buried. So the bottleneck isn't just compute, it's figuring out what representation and what objective actually extracts that structure. That's still a research problem, not a scaling problem, and that changes who is well-positioned.

The big labs clearly have the compute and the infrastructure. But their incentive structure is pulled toward products, toward whatever extends the current LLM paradigm. World models sit in an awkward place for them: expensive, long-horizon, and not obviously monetizable on a quarterly timeline. Some of them will do it seriously, and a few already are. But I don't think it's guaranteed that the best ideas come from there.

Then you have groups like Yann's effort, or various startups, that are betting specifically on this. The advantage is focus. The risk is that pre-training at the scale we're talking about, with video, is brutally expensive, and you can burn a lot of money before you know whether your objective is right. A startup gets maybe one or two real shots.

And academia, where I sit, honestly can't do the full pre-training run. We just don't have the compute. But I think academia's role is actually clearer here than it was for LLMs: we can work on the representation question, the evaluation question, what does it mean for a model to understand physics or to plan, at small scale, and those insights transfer. A lot of the recent progress in visual representation learning came from relatively small-scale experiments that later scaled.

So my honest view: the organization that succeeds will probably be one that treats this as a research problem first and a scaling problem second, and has the patience to tolerate a couple of years where the metrics don't look like anything. That's rare. It might be a lab with a protected team, it might be a well-funded startup with unusually patient investors, it might be some open consortium if the community can coordinate. I'm cautiously optimistic, mostly because the interest is real now in a way it wasn't three years ago. But I wouldn't say anyone has clearly earned the title yet.

r001.rationale: The response says startups may struggle because video pre-training is expensive, but it does not attribute robotics startups’ lack of capacity to competing demands from scaling robot hardware.

astra-6.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think the question is what we mean by a world model. If we mean a model that can generate convincing videos, that’s one level. If we mean a model that understands how actions change the world and can use that understanding to plan, that’s a much higher bar.

An organization doing this needs more than compute. It needs a strong data pipeline, people who can work across perception and decision-making, and a way to test whether the model has actually learned something useful about the world. Otherwise, it’s easy to improve visual quality without knowing whether you’re making progress on understanding.

So I wouldn’t say it has to happen at one particular kind of organization. A large lab has obvious advantages in scale. A smaller, focused team might have more freedom to rethink the objective. What I’d look for is an organization with the resources to run serious experiments and the patience to pursue a direction where the right recipe isn’t established yet.

r001.rationale: The response discusses organizational resources and compute generally, but does not attribute robotics startups’ lack of capacity to competing demands from scaling up robot hardware.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m cautiously optimistic, but I think the question is less about which organization has the most GPUs and more about which organization can sustain the right kind of research. With language models, we have a relatively clear recipe: collect text, predict the next token, and scale. For world models, we’re still figuring out what we should predict, what data we need, and how to tell whether the model has actually learned something useful about the world.

So you need compute and data, but you also need patience. An organization has to let people explore ideas that might not immediately turn into a product. A large company could do that, and a well-supported startup could too. I wouldn’t assume that the organization with the biggest resources today will necessarily discover the best approach.

The encouraging thing is that you don’t have to solve the whole problem at once. You can demonstrate a useful capability, establish a better training objective or evaluation, and build from there. I think finding an organization willing to support that process is possible. Finding one that combines the resources, the research freedom, and the patience—that’s the harder part.

r001.rationale: The response discusses compute, data, research freedom, and patience generally, but does not attribute robotics startups’ lack of capacity to competing demands from scaling robot hardware.
